facts.Observed place: Tomb of Heroes in Seraphis, just outside Ciaránach’s gates

body:
Aria’s Tomb belongs to Fein Uaill proper. The regional record explicitly corrects an earlier assumption that the tomb lies inside Ciaránach. Its association is with Aria / Pride, Knight II of Death.

A place, not a substitute for a life

The tomb gives Aria a lasting point in the landscape, but it does not resolve the competing memories of who she was, what she chose, or what others made of her death. Those questions remain in her character history.

The open record

The funeral records Aria’s preserved casket being carried into the Tomb of Heroes. Its builders, construction date, full interior, continuing custodianship and later condition remain unrecovered. The recorded burial does not date the founding of the tomb or make its supplied visual record a surveyed plan.

From the castle to the mourning city

The journey to Aria’s resting place begins after a difficult hearing at Caisleán na Brón. Bowene asks to take her body for a procession, and Draygar asks to accompany it. The company leaves its home and joins lines of people walking toward Zarathis.

The narrator stresses the walking: no teleportation, but feet and boots bringing separate lines together. As the crowds converge, the company is moved toward the front. Aria’s casket is already ahead, drawing the attention of the waiting city. The scale becomes something the companions must experience among other mourners rather than direct from outside.

The Tomb of Heroes outside Ciaránach

After hours of walking, they reach the designated tomb high in Seraphis. The narrator locates it just outside Ciaránach’s gates. This supplies a modern burial place consistent with the earlier correction: Aria’s Tomb is not inside the holy city.

Her body has been prepared and preserved for the ceremony. People are given a chance to speak before the casket is taken within. The record does not provide the tomb’s complete dimensions, the route through its interior or the history of everyone buried there. Its relationship to Aria is established by the procession and burial, not by a claim that the whole structure was newly built for her.

What the mourners carry away

Olokun approaches and apologizes quietly for being unable to help her. Draygar speaks of the love she bore her people. Bowene calls her their best and turns grief toward a demand for justice against Talan. His speech records how he wants the nation to remember her; it does not erase the different memories preserved in her character history or the last battle.

The tomb opens and the preserved casket is carried inside. The bearers return without her. Tarwen and Tyragol fall to their knees and tear their robes, and Bowene follows their example. Draygar keeps his own posture of reverence. The narrator identifies the Silver Star as the principal keepers of the tradition being followed.

When the gates close, silence holds. What feels like a night is explicitly only an hour, after which the people begin descending with muffled steps. Aria is at rest, while what comes next remains unknown. The ceremony has a witnessed ending even though its political consequences continue beyond the tomb.
